# `silk/system/system_clock`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

The `SystemClock` effect: the current date and time as Unix time, and the [`Instant`](#Instant) type that
both clocks use.

## When to use
Require `&mut SystemClock` when you need the current time to show to a person, to store, or to
send to another system, such as a timestamp in a log or a certificate check. To measure
durations, use `silk.system.monotonic_clock`, because the system time can jump.

## Details
An [`Instant`](#Instant) has signed whole seconds since `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` and a nanosecond part from
0 to 999,999,999. The system time can go forward or back when the computer adjusts its clock.
Importing this module does not install a clock. The program provides one.

## Gotchas
If a provider returns a value that is not valid, the program traps, because this effect has no
error type.

## Examples
### Provide a fixed time in a test
```silk
import silk.core.effect { Effect }
import silk.system.system_clock { Instant, SystemClock }

struct FixedClock {}

effect fn fixedNow(self: &mut FixedClock) -> Instant {
  return SystemClock.make(1700000000, 500)
}

effect fn fixedResolution(self: &mut FixedClock) -> u64 {
  return 1
}

impl SystemClock for FixedClock {
  now: FixedClock.fixedNow

  getResolution: FixedClock.fixedResolution
}

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let mut provider = FixedClock {}
  let instant = run SystemClock.now() |> Effect.provideMut<SystemClock>(&mut provider)
  if SystemClock.seconds(&instant) != 1700000000 || SystemClock.nanoseconds(&instant) != 500 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `SystemClock` with `import silk.system.system_clock { SystemClock }`.

## `Instant`

```silk
pub struct Instant
```

A point in time: signed whole seconds and a nanosecond part.

### Details

For the system clock, the seconds count from `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z`. A monotonic clock uses the
same type with an origin that it does not specify. The nanosecond part is always from 0 to
999,999,999, also for times before the origin. So `SystemClock.make(-1, 999999999)` is one
nanosecond before the origin.

<a id="SystemClock"></a>

## `SystemClock`

```silk
pub service SystemClock
```

The effect for the current date and time as Unix time.

### When to use

Require `&mut SystemClock` when you need the current time to show to a person, to store, or to
send to another system, such as a timestamp in a log or a certificate check. To measure
durations, use `silk.system.monotonic_clock`, because the system time can jump.

### Details

The time is an `Instant`: signed whole seconds since `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` and a nanosecond
part. The system time can go forward or back when the computer adjusts its clock. /// Exclusive
access lets a test provider change the time between calls. There is no operation to set the
time.

<a id="SystemClock.now"></a>

### Operation `now`

```silk
effect fn now() -> Instant ? &mut SystemClock
```

Returns the current time. It can be earlier than an earlier read, because the system time can
be adjusted.

<a id="SystemClock.getResolution"></a>

### Operation `getResolution`

```silk
effect fn getResolution() -> u64 ? &mut SystemClock
```

Returns the tick of the clock in nanoseconds. It is at least 1. The real precision can be
lower.

<a id="SystemClock.impl.make"></a>

### Associated function `make`

```silk
pub fn make(seconds: i64, nanoseconds: i64) -> Instant
```

Returns the instant `seconds` plus `nanoseconds` nanoseconds.

#### Details

Whole seconds in `nanoseconds` move into the seconds, so `SystemClock.make(0, 5000000000)` is
five seconds and `SystemClock.make(0, -1)` is one nanosecond before the origin.

#### Gotchas

A total outside the `i64` seconds range traps with an integer overflow.

<a id="SystemClock.impl.seconds"></a>

### Method `seconds`

```silk
pub fn seconds(self: &Instant) -> i64
```

Returns the whole seconds of the instant. It can be negative.

```silk
pub fn nanoseconds(self: &Instant) -> i64
```

Returns the nanosecond part of the instant, from 0 to 999,999,999.
